title: Array Probe Chemistry: On-Chip Synthesis Yield, Spacers, Density and PNA
summary: Learn how light-directed synthesis builds array probes base by base, why small per-step losses multiply into low full-length yield, how spacers and probe density change hybridization, and what a neutral PNA probe changes.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 70 Hits 4 (in situ photolithographic synthesis and 20-mer yield), 6 (probe surface density), 7 (spacer length) and 13 (PNA probes). Checked against Agbavwe 2011, Sack 2016, Lenoir 2006, Quijano 2017 and D’Agata 2017 (Europe PMC full text) and the Shchepinov 1997 abstract (full text not obtained: Europe PMC returned no full text). Hit 4: the yield arithmetic is taught as a calculation; Agbavwe 2011 reports modern stepwise coupling of about 98.5–99% and Sack 2016 ties low stepwise yield to early MeNPOC chemistry, so the reviewer’s 80–95% range is given as an illustration, not a current figure (register flag proposed). Hit 13: Quijano 2017 describes ambiguity in PNA binding direction (antiparallel vs parallel), so “only antiparallel” is not taught (register flag proposed); “rapid hybridization” was not found in the sources read. Pending: glass ~0.1 pmol/mm² and 100× polypropylene density; yield decline with over-long spacers.

objectives: Describe how light-directed in situ synthesis builds oligonucleotide probes on a chip.
Calculate the approximate full-length probe fraction from a stepwise yield and probe length.
Explain how spacer length and probe density affect hybridization yield.
State how the neutral PNA backbone changes hybridization behaviour.

scenes.title: A custom chip that glows too dimly
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a research group designs a custom oligonucleotide array. (1) Its 20-mer probes are built on the chip one base at a time, and each step works about 95% of the time. (2) The probes are attached straight onto the surface at the highest density possible. (3) A colleague suggests swapping the DNA probes for peptide nucleic acid (PNA) probes. The hybridization signal is weaker than expected. Question token: “Where did the signal go?”

cues.text: Invented scenario. A group builds a custom array, making twenty-base probes on the chip one base at a time. Each step works about ninety-five percent of the time.
The probes sit straight on the surface, packed as densely as possible.
The signal is weak, and a colleague suggests peptide nucleic acid probes. Where did the signal go?

scenes.title: Building probes with light
scenes.altText: Schematic of light-directed in situ synthesis on a glass surface. Card 1: each growing probe ends in a light-removable (photolabile) 5′ protecting group. Card 2: light, patterned by a physical mask (Affymetrix) or by micromirrors (maskless synthesis), removes the protecting group only on chosen spots. Card 3: the next phosphoramidite base couples only where the chain was deprotected; the cycle repeats once per base. Card 4: a failed coupling that is not capped, or a failed deprotection, leaves a probe missing a base (a deletion); in maskless synthesis, stray light can also add an unwanted base (an insertion).

cues.text: Light-directed synthesis builds each probe directly on the chip. Every growing chain is capped by a protecting group that light can remove.
Light, shaped by a mask or by tiny mirrors, uncaps only the chosen spots. Affymetrix chips use physical masks; maskless systems use mirrors.
The next base then couples only where the chain was uncapped, and the cycle repeats once for every base in the probe.
If a base fails to couple and the chain is not capped, or a cap is not removed, that probe ends up missing a base, a deletion. Stray light can also add an unwanted base, an insertion.

scenes.title: Small losses multiply
scenes.altText: Calculation card: the fraction of full-length, correct probes is roughly the stepwise yield raised to the number of steps. For a 20-mer: 95% per step → 0.95^20 ≈ 36%; 80% per step → 0.80^20 ≈ 1%; 99% per step → 0.99^20 ≈ 82% (arithmetic only). History card: early photolabile groups (MeNPOC) gave relatively low stepwise yields, which limited arrays to short probes; NPPOC gave almost quantitative coupling; one maskless-synthesis study measured average stepwise coupling efficiencies of about 98.5–99%, but found the effective stepwise yield lower than coupling efficiency alone, because deprotection and stray light also cause errors. Longer probes lower the overall yield.

cues.text: Every step must succeed for a probe to be right, so the yields multiply. The share of full-length probes is about the step yield raised to the number of steps.
For a twenty-mer at ninety-five percent per step, that is about thirty-six percent. At eighty percent per step, only about one percent is correct.

Early light-removable groups gave fairly low step yields, so early arrays used short probes. Newer chemistry pushed coupling close to complete. One maskless study measured coupling of about ninety-eight and a half to ninety-nine percent per step.

But coupling is only part of each step. The same study found the real step yield lower than coupling alone, because uncapping and stray light add errors. And the longer the probe, the lower the overall yield.

scenes.title: Room to hybridize, and a neutral probe
scenes.altText: Three cards from surface and probe chemistry. Spacer card: in one study on an amine-functionalised polypropylene support, spacers of at least 40 atoms between the support and the oligonucleotide gave up to a 150-fold increase in hybridization yield; charged groups in the spacer reduced the yield. Density card: when probes are too close together, steric hindrance lowers hybridization; the highest yields came at about 50% of the maximum oligonucleotide density. PNA card: peptide nucleic acid has an uncharged pseudopeptide backbone, which reviews link to more stable PNA–DNA duplexes; a single mismatch lowers the melting temperature more (about 15 °C vs 4 °C for DNA–DNA), binding is insensitive to ionic strength, and PNA resists enzymatic degradation, including by nucleases. Hook answers card.

cues.text: Surface chemistry matters too. In one study, a spacer of at least forty atoms between the support and the probe raised hybridization yield up to a hundred and fifty-fold. Charged groups in the spacer lowered it.
Crowding hurts. When probes sit too close together, they block each other, and the best yield came at about half the maximum probe density.

Peptide nucleic acid probes have an uncharged backbone, and they bind DNA more tightly. A single mismatch drops the melting temperature more than in DNA, binding barely depends on salt, and they resist enzymatic breakdown.
Back to the hook: errors multiplied over twenty steps, there was no spacer, and the probes were too crowded. PNA probes could sharpen mismatch discrimination, but they do not fix synthesis yield.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “95% per step means 95% of probes are correct” (✓ yields multiply: about 36% of 20-mers); “Pack probes as densely as possible” (✓ crowding causes steric hindrance; the best yield came at about half the maximum density); “PNA hybridizes like DNA, only stronger” (✓ PNA has a neutral backbone, its binding is insensitive to ionic strength, and a single mismatch costs more).

cues.text: Trap one: ninety-five percent per step means ninety-five percent of probes are right. No: the yields multiply, so only about a third of twenty-mers are full length.
Trap two: pack the probes as densely as possible. No: crowded probes block each other. The best yield came at about half the maximum density.
Trap three: PNA is just stronger DNA. No: it has a neutral backbone, its binding is insensitive to salt, and a single mismatch costs more.

props.title: ✗ “Densest is best.”
lines: ✓ Crowding hinders; best ~50% of max (one study)

scenes.title: Gates, ladder, elbow room
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Every base is a GATE the probe must pass, so multiply the gates; a SPACER is a ladder that lifts the probe off the floor; probes need ELBOW ROOM; PNA is an uncharged probe that grips harder and punishes mismatches.” Tokens: gates multiply · ladder = spacer · elbow room = density. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: every base is a gate the probe must pass, so multiply the gates. A spacer is a ladder lifting the probe off the floor, and probes need elbow room. PNA is an uncharged probe that grips harder and punishes mismatches.

Where it breaks: real errors also include insertions and partial uncapping, and yields differ by base. The spacer and density optimums come from one support in one study. And PNA can bind in more than one orientation.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Full-length probes ≈ (step yield)ⁿ: 95% per step → ~36% of 20-mers”, “Spacer ≥40 atoms · ~half maximum density · PNA = neutral, salt-insensitive, mismatch-sensitive”.

cues.text: Synthesis yields multiply with every base, so a twenty-mer made at ninety-five percent per step is only about one-third full length, and hybridization also improves with a long spacer, uncrowded probes and, for specificity, a neutral peptide nucleic acid probe.

props.label: Spacer ≥ 40 atoms · ~½ max density · PNA neutral

explanation.what: Plain language: some arrays build each probe on the chip one letter at a time, using light to choose which spots get the next letter. Every step can fail, so the losses add up. How the probe is held on the surface, and how crowded the probes are, also change how well the sample sticks. PNA is an uncharged DNA look-alike that sticks more tightly and more selectively. Scientific terms: in situ light-directed (photolithographic) synthesis, photolabile 5′ protecting group (MeNPOC, NPPOC), physical mask, maskless array synthesis (micromirrors), phosphoramidite coupling, stepwise yield, deletion error, spacer (linker), surface coverage, steric hindrance, peptide nucleic acid (PNA), melting temperature (Tm).
explanation.why: A probe is correct only if every coupling and every deprotection succeeds, so the full-length fraction falls roughly as the stepwise yield to the power of the number of steps. Probes right on the support, or crowded together, are sterically hindered from pairing with the target. PNA has an uncharged pseudopeptide backbone in place of the negatively charged phosphodiester backbone, which reviews link to more stable PNA–DNA duplexes.
explanation.measure: Full-length fraction ≈ (stepwise yield)ⁿ: 20-mer at 95% → ~36%; at 80% → ~1%; at 99% → ~82% (arithmetic only). One maskless study: average stepwise coupling ~98.5–99%, with the effective stepwise yield lower than coupling efficiency because deprotection and stray light also cause errors. Shchepinov 1997 (polypropylene support): spacer ≥40 atoms, up to 150-fold more hybridization; charged spacer groups reduce yield; best yield at ~50% of maximum oligonucleotide density. PNA: single mismatch lowers Tm about 15 °C vs about 4 °C in DNA/DNA.
explanation.differs: In situ synthesis (built on the chip, yield limited by stepwise chemistry) vs deposited probes (made off-chip, then spotted); physical mask (Affymetrix) vs maskless micromirrors; DNA probe (negatively charged, smaller mismatch penalty) vs PNA probe (neutral, salt-insensitive, larger mismatch penalty, nuclease-resistant).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: compute the correct-sequence fraction from a per-step yield (e.g. 0.95 to the 20th power), recognise that a spacer raises hybridization and that over-dense probes lower it, or pick the PNA property that follows from its neutral backbone.

questions.stem: A 20-mer probe is synthesized in situ with an average stepwise yield of 95%. About what fraction of the probes at each feature are full length?

options.rationale: Correct. 0.95 raised to the 20th power is about 0.36, because every step must succeed.
Incorrect. That is the yield of a single step, not of all 20 steps together.
Incorrect. About 82% corresponds to 99% per step (0.99 to the 20th power).
Incorrect. About 1% corresponds to 80% per step (0.80 to the 20th power).

questions.stem: In a study of oligonucleotide arrays on a polypropylene support, hybridization yield was highest at about half of the maximum oligonucleotide surface density. What best explains this?

options.text: Probes packed too closely sterically hinder one another’s pairing with the target
options.rationale: Correct. The study names steric hindrance between closely spaced oligonucleotides.

options.text: Lower density raises the stepwise synthesis yield of each probe
options.rationale: Incorrect. Surface coverage was varied with linkers; the effect described is on hybridization, not synthesis chemistry.

options.text: Fewer probes lower the melting temperature of the duplex
options.rationale: Incorrect. The study attributes the lower yield at high coverage to steric hindrance between neighbouring probes, not to a change in duplex melting temperature.

options.text: Dense probes bind too much labeled target and saturate the scanner
options.rationale: Incorrect. The study measured lower hybridization yield at high coverage, not a detector limit.

questions.stem: Which property of a peptide nucleic acid (PNA) probe follows from its uncharged backbone?

options.text: Its duplexes with DNA are more stable than the matching DNA–DNA duplexes
options.rationale: Correct. Reviews attribute the greater stability of PNA–DNA complexes to the uncharged backbone.

options.text: It tolerates single-base mismatches better than DNA does
options.rationale: Incorrect. A single mismatch lowers Tm more in PNA–DNA (about 15 °C) than in DNA–DNA (about 4 °C).

options.text: It is rapidly degraded by nucleases
options.rationale: Incorrect. The unnatural pseudopeptide backbone makes PNA resistant to enzymatic degradation, including by nucleases.

options.text: It needs high salt to bind its target
options.rationale: Incorrect. PNA is described as insensitive to ionic strength, so it does not need high salt to bind.

references.usedFor: Europe PMC full text. Light-directed synthesis cycle with a photolabile 5′-OH group; Affymetrix uses physical masks; coupling failure or 5′-deprotection failure gives a deletion (dominant error); in maskless synthesis insertions from stray light also contribute significantly; measured stepwise coupling about 98.5–99% (per base 98.0–99.8%); stepwise coupling efficiency is higher than the average stepwise yield calculated from the full-length fraction; overall yield lower for long oligonucleotide arrays; early MeNPOC coupling 92–94%.

references.usedFor: Europe PMC full text. In situ methods based on phosphoramidite chemistry; early MeNPOC groups gave relatively low stepwise yield, limiting arrays to short oligomers; NPPOC gave almost quantitative coupling.

Amine-functionalised polypropylene support; optimal spacer at least 40 atoms, up to 150-fold more hybridization; charged spacer groups diminish yield; steric hindrance when oligonucleotides are too close; highest yield at about 50% of maximum oligonucleotide concentration.

references.citation: Quijano E, Bahal R, Ricciardi A, Saltzman WM, Glazer PM. Therapeutic Peptide Nucleic Acids: Principles, Limitations, and Opportunities. Yale J Biol Med. 2017;90(4):583-598.

Pseudopeptide backbone is charge neutral, giving stronger hybridization; less tolerant of base pair mismatches; resistant to enzymatic degradation (nuclease resistance); bis-PNA binds one strand antiparallel and one parallel (Hoogsteen); constrained PNAs reduce ambiguity in binding direction (antiparallel vs parallel).

references.usedFor: Europe PMC full text. Uncharged backbone makes PNA/DNA complexes more stable than DNA/DNA; insensitive to ionic strength and pH; resistant to enzymatic cleavage; single mismatch lowers Tm about 15 °C vs 4 °C in DNA/DNA.

claims.text: Light-directed in situ synthesis: photolabile 5′ cap, mask or micromirrors, base-by-base coupling; deletions from failed (uncapped) coupling or deprotection; insertions from stray light.
Full-length fraction falls with probe length as the stepwise yields multiply (20-mer: ~36% at 95%, ~1% at 80%, ~82% at 99%).
claims.note: The percentages are arithmetic (yield to the 20th power); the source supports that overall correct-sequence yield falls with length and depends on stepwise yield.

claims.text: Early MeNPOC chemistry gave low stepwise yields; NPPOC near-quantitative; one maskless study measured ~98.5–99% stepwise coupling, with the effective stepwise yield lower than coupling efficiency.
Spacer of at least 40 atoms gives up to 150-fold more hybridization; charged spacer groups lower yield.
Crowded probes cause steric hindrance; best yield at about 50% of maximum density.
PNA: neutral backbone, more stable duplexes, salt-insensitive, larger mismatch Tm penalty (~15 vs 4 °C), resistant to enzymatic degradation.
Reviewer: probe surface density on glass ~0.1 pmol/mm², ~100× less than aminated polypropylene; over-long spacers reduce yield.
claims.note: Not found in the sources read (Shchepinov 1997 full text not obtained); not taught.

claims.text: Reviewer: PNA hybridizes rapidly and recognises only antiparallel single strands.
claims.note: Rapid hybridization not found in the sources read; Quijano 2017 describes antiparallel/parallel ambiguity. Not taught.

claims.text: Scenario invented; chip and probe drawings schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 70 Hit 4 gives 80–95% photodeprotection efficiency per cycle (1–36% correct 20-mers) as a general figure. Sack 2016 ties low stepwise yield to early MeNPOC chemistry, and Agbavwe 2011 measured about 98.5–99% stepwise coupling in modern maskless synthesis (versus 92–94% for early MeNPOC chemistry), while noting that the effective stepwise yield is lower than coupling efficiency; stepwise yield depends on coupling and deprotection, not photodeprotection alone (register flag rv-photolitho-stepwise-yield).

Ch. 70 Hit 13 says PNA gives “only antiparallel single-strand recognition”. Quijano 2017 describes ambiguity in PNA binding direction (antiparallel vs parallel) and bis-PNAs whose second strand binds parallel by Hoogsteen pairing; the lesson does not teach “only antiparallel” (register flag rv-pna-binding-direction).
